clue.text: Famous director on set shooting film in Nadsat?

indicators.note: on places the director's name after the letter from set
shooting is read as starting off, so only the opening letter of set is taken

parts.note: Fritz Lang, director of Metropolis and M

explanation.surface: A great film director is on set, shooting a picture whose dialogue is in an invented teen argot.
explanation.walkthrough: Nadsat is the invented teenage argot of Anthony Burgess's A Clockwork Orange; the question mark marks it as an example of the category.
explanation.definitionFit: Nadsat is an example of street jargon, the invented gang speech of Burgess's droogs.

clue.text: Fast-written piece us cats rap about

indicators.note: about means the letters of the three words are scattered around into a new order

explanation.surface: A hastily written item in which some American cats rap.
explanation.walkthrough: Fast is not about speed: Howard Fast wrote the novel about the rebel gladiator.
explanation.definitionFit: Howard Fast's 1951 novel about the slave revolt is titled after its gladiator hero.

clue.text: As much as one likes a mad diary writer, there's no need for flannel in the end!

indicators.note: there's no need for says a letter is dropped from the writer's name

parts.note: Nikolai Gogol wrote The Diary of a Madman

indicators.note: in the end picks out the closing letter of flannel

explanation.surface: Someone happily reading a lunatic's journal decides fine words are unnecessary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a mad diary writer' is really A plus GOGOL, author of The Diary of a Madman; dropping the L that ends 'flannel' leaves GOGO.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means in abundance or without limit, as in 'drinks galore'.

clue.text: Graduate, on checking into hotel, is happy to meet Mick Jagger?

parts.note: to be happy is to be glad
Mick Jagger is a Rolling Stone; the question mark flags the example

explanation.surface: A new graduate checking into a hotel is thrilled to bump into the Rolling Stones' singer.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a picture: a graduate checking in carries a Gladstone, the hinged leather travelling bag.
explanation.definitionFit: A Gladstone bag is the hinged leather case a traveller carries when checking into a hotel, cryptically pictured here.

clue.text: She had to be thrifty with gas and energy up

indicators.note: up here means in disorder, so the letters of the two words are mixed

explanation.surface: A careful householder had to economise on gas and energy bills.
explanation.walkthrough: Anne Brontë's heroine is a poor clergyman's daughter who becomes a governess to help her impoverished family.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Brontë's governess heroine grows up in a family forced into frugal living after her father's losses.

clue.text: Party host in huge trouble after bit of argy-bargy

indicators.note: after says the other pieces come behind the letter from argy-bargy
bit of takes only the first letter of the following word

parts.note: huge means big
to ail is to trouble or afflict

explanation.surface: Someone hosting a party is in great difficulty after a quarrel breaks out.
explanation.walkthrough: Mike Leigh's play Abigail's Party is named after the teenager whose party is going on next door; argy-bargy is British slang for a noisy squabble.
explanation.definitionFit: In Mike Leigh's play, the girl giving the off-stage teenage party lends the work its title.

clue.text: Poetic type of lover on time with a couple of lines

parts.note: a nut is an enthusiast or lover, as in a jazz nut
L is line, so two of them give LL

explanation.surface: A romantic suitor writes verse, keeping to time with a couple of lines.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeff Nuttall was a British poet and counter-culture figure, author of Bomb Culture.
explanation.definitionFit: Jeff Nuttall was an English performance poet, so he is a verse-writing sort.

clue.text: Part of a play imagined for broadcast on the radio

indicators.note: broadcast on the radio means heard rather than read, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: something imagined is seen in the mind's eye

explanation.surface: A section of a drama, conjured up for transmission on air.
explanation.definitionFit: A play is divided into acts and these smaller units of continuous action.

clue.text: "If I cannot move heaven, I will -" (Virgil)

definitions.text: "If I cannot move heaven, I will -" (Virgil)

parts.words: "If I cannot move heaven, I will -" (Virgil)
parts.note: Juno's threat in the Aeneid, Book 7, 'flectere si nequeo superos, Acheronta movebo', completed in English with its usual phrase for the underworld

explanation.surface: A quotation from Virgil's Aeneid with its closing words missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Fill in the familiar English rendering of Juno's line: if she cannot sway the gods above, she will stir up the underworld.
explanation.definitionFit: To cause uproar is the idiom, here taken literally as stirring the underworld, Acheron.

clue.text: Heart-wrenching Irish poet or an American writer

indicators.note: heart-wrenching says the middle of the poet's name is twisted, one letter moved within it

parts.note: W. B. Yeats, the Irish poet

explanation.surface: A moving poem by an Irish writer, or the work of an American novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Shift the E of YEATS two places along to get the surname of Richard Yates, author of Revolutionary Road.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Yates, the American novelist of Revolutionary Road, bears this surname.

clue.text: A way in which lesson is given to one Luke Rhinehart?

parts.note: a moral is the lesson of a story
I is the Roman numeral for one
ST is short for street, a way

explanation.surface: A route through which a lesson is taught to the author of The Dice Man.
explanation.walkthrough: Luke Rhinehart is the pen name of George Cockcroft, whose novel The Dice Man has a hero who abandons all morality to the throw of a die.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dice Man's author championed living by chance with no moral rules, the mark of someone without ethical principles.

clue.text: Nobel-prize winner reviewing work by European

indicators.note: reviewing is taken as viewing again from the other end, so the word is turned around

parts.note: toil is hard work

explanation.surface: A Nobel laureate is critiquing a piece by a European author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reviewing' looks like criticism but is the reversal signal, working on 'work' alone; 'by European' puts the E in front.
explanation.definitionFit: T. S. Eliot won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1948.

clue.text: Devices in Orton play around front of stage

indicators.note: around means the title is turned round to read backwards

parts.note: Loot is a farce by Joe Orton

indicators.note: front of takes the opening letter of stage

explanation.surface: Props used in a production of an Orton play wheeled to the front of the stage.
explanation.walkthrough: Joe Orton's farce Loot is turned by 'around'; 'in' is only a link, not a container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Implements and instruments are both devices for doing a job.

clue.text: What Hal has in a conflict: ultimately impulsive head

parts.note: a war is a conflict

indicators.note: ultimately takes the final letter of impulsive

parts.note: a ness is a headland, a head projecting into the sea

explanation.surface: Prince Hal, in a war, shows himself rash and impetuous in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: Hal suggests Shakespeare's prince but is the self-conscious computer HAL 9000 of 2001: A Space Odyssey.
explanation.definitionFit: HAL 9000 is a computer with consciousness, knowing its own existence and its surroundings.

clue.text: Nonsense producer heard in hymn celebrating Christ's birth

indicators.note: heard says the word is taken for its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: a Christmas carol celebrates the Nativity

explanation.surface: A piece of absurdity is overheard within a Christmas hymn.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll wrote Jabberwocky and other celebrated nonsense verse.

clue.text: Colonel Markham Everard is one portly person in charge

parts.note: portly means round or stout
a head is the person in charge

explanation.surface: A colonel is described as a stout figure who commands.
explanation.walkthrough: Colonel Markham Everard is the Parliamentarian officer in Walter Scott's novel Woodstock, set in the English Civil War.
explanation.definitionFit: Everard fights for Parliament in Scott's Woodstock, so he is one of Cromwell's party in the Civil War.

clue.text: You might say Enid of St Jude and Jesus regret ignoring odds

definitions.text: You might say Enid of St Jude

parts.note: Jesus is the Lamb of God

indicators.note: ignoring odds means the odd-placed letters of regret are dropped, keeping the even ones

explanation.surface: A churchgoer's regret over religious matters, involving a saint and Christ.
explanation.walkthrough: Enid is the matriarch of Jonathan Franzen's The Corrections, living in the fictional town of St Jude; 'regret' minus its first, third and fifth letters leaves ERT.
explanation.definitionFit: Enid's married surname in Franzen's The Corrections is that of the family at the novel's centre.

clue.text: Vain model portrayed differently in Hollywood?

indicators.note: portrayed differently says the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A conceited model is shown in a new light in Tinseltown.
explanation.definitionFit: Hollywood is the prime example of the film world, the realm of the cinema industry.

clue.text: After hospital admission, Echo sent off Reuven Malter's story

indicators.note: admission means letting the hospital letter in among the others
off means the letters of the two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: Once admitted to hospital, the nymph Echo was dispatched to tell a boy's tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' shuffles ECHOSENT into TECHOSEN; 'admission' lets H in after the T. Reuven Malter narrates Chaim Potok's novel of Brooklyn friendship.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaim Potok's 1967 novel is narrated by Reuven Malter, so it is his story.

clue.text: Cruel headmaster is out of sorts aboard ship

indicators.note: aboard puts the other piece inside the letters for ship

parts.note: SS is short for steamship
queer, in older British use, means unwell or out of sorts

explanation.surface: A harsh schoolmaster feels poorly while on board a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: Wackford Squeers runs the brutal Dotheboys Hall school in Dickens's Nicholas Nickleby.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's Dotheboys Hall is run by Wackford, a brutal schoolmaster who beats and starves his pupils.

clue.text: Unless author's quiet, one's grabbing extremely large dishpan primarily

parts.note: sh is the call for quiet

indicators.note: grabbing means the letters for one's close around the other letters

parts.note: one is I, and the 's adds S

indicators.note: primarily takes the first letter of each of the three words before it

explanation.surface: A writer wonders whether to keep silent while someone seizes a huge washing-up bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: Unless is not a conjunction here but the title of Carol Shields's last novel; 'primarily' works on 'extremely' as well as 'large' and 'dishpan'.
explanation.definitionFit: Carol Shields, the Canadian novelist, wrote Unless (2002), so she is that book's writer.

clue.text: Southeastern town in France where Shenstone saw a miracle

parts.note: ville is French for town

explanation.surface: A town in the southeast of France where a poet witnessed something miraculous.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a French town, but the answer is the Spanish city; William Shenstone's poem 'The Miracle at Seville' is not needed if the wordplay is followed.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish city in Andalusia is the setting of the miracle in the poem.

clue.text: Romantic writer and how he could describe a clam, I'm told

indicators.note: I'm told says the description is given by its sound

parts.words: how he could describe a clam
parts.note: a clam has a hard casing, so it could be called shelly

explanation.surface: A Romantic poet, and a word he might use for a shellfish, so it is said.
explanation.walkthrough: Percy Bysshe Shelley was a leading English Romantic poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Percy Bysshe Shelley was a leading poet of the English Romantic movement.

clue.text: European Nobel prize-winner reading English novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so the letters are put into a fresh order

parts.note: reading as written, with English giving E; the setter needs a D as well

explanation.surface: A Continental laureate is getting through a new book from England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' signals the anagram, but READING plus E (English) gives eight letters with one D; the answer needs a second D, a slip in the printed clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The French writer of The Immoralist won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1947.

clue.text: Religious sorts Old Devil's writer drunkenly picked up

indicators.note: drunkenly picked up means the name is heard as a tipsy speaker would slur it, the s blurring

parts.note: Kingsley Amis wrote The Old Devils, which won the 1986 Booker Prize

explanation.surface: Pious folk collected a drunk novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: Slurred, as a drunk would say it, AMIS comes out with a hissing sh at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: The Anabaptist communities of Pennsylvania are a devout group of Christians.

clue.text: Singer bursting into piece from Europe, Love or Muse

indicators.note: bursting into puts the singer inside the other pieces
piece from takes the first letter of Europe

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, O
a rat sings to the police, as an informer

explanation.surface: A vocalist breaks into a European piece about love or inspiration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' looks like a vocalist but is an informer who 'sings', a RAT.
explanation.definitionFit: Erato is the Greek Muse of love poetry.

clue.text: Want to skip opening in Hugo-nominated Sci-fi book

indicators.note: to skip opening means the word for want loses its first letter

parts.note: a dearth is a want or lack

explanation.surface: A craving to miss the opening of an award-nominated science fiction novel.
explanation.walkthrough: David Brin's novel Earth was nominated for the Hugo Award in 1991.
explanation.definitionFit: David Brin's 1990 novel shares its name with our planet and was a Hugo finalist.

clue.text: In which Rigg escapes and legs it around India

indicators.note: around puts the other letters on either side of India's letter

parts.note: to leg it is to run, so legs it is runs
I is India in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: An actress flees and dashes about the subcontinent.
explanation.walkthrough: Rigg looks like the actress but refers to a fugitive who hides out among crumbling remains.
explanation.definitionFit: Crumbling remains of buildings make a natural hiding place for a fugitive.

clue.text: Some tire Nantucket woman who vowed to save Jewish people

definitions.text: woman who vowed to save Jewish people

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Some tired person from Nantucket is a woman sworn to rescue Jews.
explanation.walkthrough: Irena Sendler smuggled Jewish children out of the Warsaw Ghetto.
explanation.definitionFit: Irena Sendler, a Polish social worker, pledged to rescue Jewish children from the Warsaw Ghetto.

clue.text: LA bullies working as assistants in knocking out kids

indicators.note: working means the letters are put to work in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Los Angeles thugs employed as helpers in beating up children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knocking out kids' sounds violent but means sending children to sleep.
explanation.definitionFit: Soothing songs help put children to sleep, so they assist in getting them off.

clue.text: "No heavings hint that winds have been / On seas less — serene" (Poe)

definitions.text: "No heavings hint that winds have been / On seas less — serene" (Poe)

parts.words: "No heavings hint that winds have been / On seas less — serene" (Poe)
parts.note: lines from Poe's The City in the Sea, with the adverb before serene left out for the solver to supply

explanation.surface: A quotation from Poe's poem The City in the Sea with one word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: Supply the adverb Poe uses to describe the unnaturally calm, sinister sea around his doomed city.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing adverb means in a repulsive or dreadful manner, Poe's word for the unsettling calm.

clue.text: Flipping inquisitive Dutch linesman

indicators.note: flipping means the word is turned over to read backwards

parts.note: nosy means inquisitive

explanation.surface: An annoyingly curious Dutch assistant referee.
explanation.walkthrough: Linesman is not a football official but a writer of lines: Edward Dyson was an Australian poet and balladeer.
explanation.definitionFit: A writer of verse lines, such as the Australian balladeer Edward Dyson, is cryptically a man of lines.
